claim.pdf_says:
15.8.2   General format

  FUNCTION  ACOS  ( argument-1 )      [FUNCTION and ACOS are both UNDERLINED in the printed general format]
claim.why_it_matters: Underlining in a general format is normative notation (5.2.6): an underlined word is a REQUIRED word. The transcription drops the underline on both FUNCTION and ACOS and wraps the format in a fenced code block instead. specs/ISO_COBOL.md line 34068. The house convention everywhere else in clause 15 is `<u>FUNCTION</u> <u>NAME</u>` (e.g. ABS line 34026, ANNUITY line 34102, ATAN line 34190), so any tool or reader deriving required-vs-optional words from the markup reads FUNCTION/ACOS as non-required here while reading them as required three formats away.

verdict.reasoning:
INDEPENDENTLY CONFIRMED at the glyph level, but the claim's characterization of scope is wrong.

WHAT I SAW IN THE PDF. Rendered page 847 at 300 dpi and cropped/upscaled the 15.8.2 general-format line (E:/Temp/specrecon/v847/crop_fmt.png). The printed line reads `FUNCTION  ACOS  ( argument-1 )`. There are two distinct horizontal rules beneath the text: one spanning exactly the eight glyphs of FUNCTION, a separate one spanning exactly the four glyphs of ACOS. The rules are broken between the two words (they are two underlines, not one continuous rule), and `( argument-1 )` carries no rule at all. So the printed format underlines FUNCTION and ACOS and nothing else. The claim quotes the PDF accurately.

WHAT IS IN THE MARKDOWN. specs/ISO_COBOL.md lines 34067-34069 are exactly:
  34067 ```
  34068 FUNCTION ACOS ( argument-1 )
  34069 ```
No <u> markup, no compensating annotation. The claim quotes the markdown accurately and cites the right line.

WHY THIS IS NOT MERE FORMATTING. Underlining is not typography here, it is the standard's own meta-language. specs/ISO_COBOL.md line 2631: \"Keywords ... are shown in uppercase and underlined in general formats. They are required...\" Line 2644: \"Optional words ... are shown in uppercase and not underlined in general formats. They may be written to add clarity...\" A consumer applying that rule to the transcribed line derives the opposite of the truth: that FUNCTION and ACOS are optional words that \"may be written to add clarity\", i.e. that `( argument-1 )` alone is a valid function-identifier. That is a change in derivable meaning, not page-break furniture, wrapping, or hyphenation. So it clears the rejection bar.

WHERE THE CLAIM IS WRONG. The stated rationale -- that `<u>FUNCTION</u> <u>NAME</u>` is \"the house convention everywhere else in clause 15\", making ACOS an anomalous one-off sitting three formats away from correct neighbours -- is false. Counting the whole of clause 15 (lines 34009-38781, the ABS..YEAR-TO-YYYY function descriptions): 20 general formats use `<u>FUNCTION</u>`, and 53 are bare un-underlined `FUNCTION ...` lines (26 of those inside fenced code blocks, 27 as plain paragraph lines). Only 2 of the 53 carry any compensating figure-note or prose statement about underlining. The underline-preserving form is therefore the MINORITY treatment (20 of 73), and ACOS is one instance of a systematic transcription gap, not a local inconsistency. The three neighbours the claim cites (ABS 34026, ANNUITY 34102, ATAN 34190) do all use `<u>`, so those spot-checks are individually correct -- but generalizing from them to \"everywhere else\" is not.

TWO FURTHER CORRECTIONS. (1) The fenced code block is not itself the defect. 26 other clause-15 formats are fenced and fencing usefully preserves the significant intra-format spacing; the fence is merely the vehicle that makes inline <u> unrepresentable. The substantive loss is the underlining. (2) The practical blast radius for THIS format specifically is bounded: `FUNCTION ACOS ( argument-1 )` contains no optional words at all, so no required-vs-optional ambiguity arises among the words actually present -- every token is required. The harm is that markup-driven extraction mis-classifies FUNCTION and ACOS as non-keywords, not that a reader could mis-parse which parts of the format are elective. Formats such as BYTE-LENGTH and LENGTH (`FUNCTION LENGTH ( argument-1 [ PHYSICAL ] )`), which are also transcribed bare, are the higher-risk members of the same pattern because there the underline distinguishes a required word inside an optional bracket.

Net: the discrepancy is real and is a genuine loss of normative notation, but it should be filed as one instance of a clause-wide systematic gap affecting ~53 function general formats, not as a localized figure error on page 847.
verdict.corrected_description: Page 847, 15.8.2 ACOS general format. The printed standard sets `FUNCTION  ACOS  ( argument-1 )` with two separate underlines, one under FUNCTION and one under ACOS; `( argument-1 )` is not underlined. specs/ISO_COBOL.md lines 34067-34069 transcribe this as a fenced code block containing bare `FUNCTION ACOS ( argument-1 )`, dropping both underlines with no compensating figure note. Underlining is normative notation -- the transcription's own text at lines 2631 and 2644 states that underlined uppercase words in a general format are required keywords and non-underlined uppercase words are optional words -- so a markup-driven consumer derives that FUNCTION and ACOS are optional, the opposite of the truth. CORRECTION TO THE ORIGINAL REPORT: this is not an isolated deviation from a consistent clause-15 convention. Across clause 15 (lines 34009-38781) only 20 function general formats preserve `<u>FUNCTION</u>`, while 53 are transcribed bare (26 fenced, 27 plain), with only 2 of those 53 carrying any prose note about underlining. ACOS is one instance of a systematic clause-wide gap and should be remediated as such. Also note the fenced block itself is not the defect -- fencing preserves the significant intra-format spacing and is used for 26 other formats -- the defect is solely the dropped underlining; and for ACOS specifically the format contains no optional words, so the loss mis-labels keywords rather than creating an in-format required/optional ambiguity (formats like `FUNCTION LENGTH ( argument-1 [ PHYSICAL ] )`, transcribed bare in the same pattern, carry the higher risk).
